gaps.text: In-line measurement of product temperature with temperature sensor
In-line measurement of product texture / scattering state with in-line viscosity or consistency sensor

Combining several spectroscopy methods (data fusion) (Low-level fusion: the two scaled spectral blocks are joined into one matrix so that neither method dominates the model. Both probes have to look at the same product volume at the same time, and the two data streams must be brought to one common time step. Each method keeps its own calibration and diagnostics, and the fused model is only worth keeping if it beats the better single method on independent runs.)

The enquiry asks for earlier composition information; the supplied pages give no accuracy, repeatability, detection-limit or response-time figure for fat or protein in milk or a concentrated milk product.

items.finding: The source states that temperature sensitivity of the OH bands is a severe drawback for measuring aqueous solution in NIR and MIR, so tempered sample holders are necessary.
items.how_it_applies: This could inform the assessment by supporting temperature measurement or control alongside NIR and MIR, and by suggesting tests under the temperature variation seen in production.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The source is a review about biopharmaceutical downstream processing and aqueous solutions, not concentrated milk or an in-line milk line; transfer to a food matrix and in-line probe needs testing.

citation.quote: Additionally, the temperature sensitivity of the OH bands is a severe drawback for measuring aqueous solution in NIR and MIR, which makes tempered sample holders necessary [29].
citation.label: E02 ¶12

items.finding: The source describes low-level data fusion as the simplest way to combine inputs by rearranging data into a new matrix with variables from different sources placed one after the other.
items.how_it_applies: This supports the O3 low-level fusion concept, but the assessment should verify that the two spectral blocks are aligned and that the fused model is compared with the better single method.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The source is a PAT data-fusion review, not a milk or concentrated-milk study, and it does not establish performance for NIR and MIR on this product.

citation.quote: Low-level data fusion (LLDF) is considered the simplest method to achieve a combination of inputs. In this case, the data is rearranged into a new data matrix, where the variables coming from different sources are placed one after the other.
citation.label: E03 ¶31

items.finding: The source says that before fusing data from multiple sources, it is essential to evaluate each dataset's contribution to the model and its complementarity.
items.how_it_applies: This could inform the comparison experiment by requiring independent runs that test whether adding the second method improves the model over the better single method.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The source is a review and does not provide milk-specific or in-line validation; complementarity must be demonstrated on the customer's product.

citation.quote: Before fusing data from multiple sources, it is essential to evaluate the contribution of each dataset to the model and its complementarity.
citation.label: E03 ¶82

items.finding: The source states that AOAC International guidelines specify performance parameters including LOD, LOQ, recovery, repeatability, reproducibility, and probability of detection for screening methods.
items.how_it_applies: This could inform the assessment by indicating which performance figures should be requested or measured for fat and protein, though the source gives no such figures for milk.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The source concerns HSI for mycotoxin monitoring in food, not milk fat or protein or an in-line milk process; the validation framework may not transfer directly.

citation.quote: The AOAC International provides standardized guidelines for method validation through its Official Methods of Analysis program, which specifies performance parameters including limit of detection (LOD), limit of quantification (LOQ), recovery, repeatability, reproducibility, and probability of detection for screening methods [67].
citation.label: E04 ¶62
